{{Short description|Logical formulation of recursion}}
In [[mathematical logic]], '''fixed-point logics''' are extensions of classical predicate logic that have been introduced to express recursion. Their development has been motivated by [[descriptive complexity theory]] and their relationship to [[Database query language|database query languages]], in particular to [[Datalog]].

Least fixed-point logic was first studied systematically by [[Yiannis N. Moschovakis]] in 1974,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Moschovakis |first=Yiannis N. |author-link=Yiannis N. Moschovakis |date=1974 |title=Elementary Induction on Abstract Structures |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/s0049-237x(08)x7092-2 |journal=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics |volume=77 |doi=10.1016/s0049-237x(08)x7092-2 |isbn=9780444105370 |issn=0049-237X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and it was introduced to computer scientists in 1979, when [[Alfred Aho]] and [[Jeffrey Ullman]]  suggested fixed-point logic as an expressive database query language.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Aho|first1=Alfred V.|last2=Ullman|first2=Jeffrey D.|title=Proceedings of the 6th ACM SIGACT-SIGPLAN symposium on Principles of programming languages - POPL '79 |chapter=Universality of data retrieval languages |date=1979 |pages=110–119|location=New York, New York, USA|publisher=ACM Press|doi=10.1145/567752.567763|s2cid=3242505|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Partial fixed-point logic ==
For a [[Signature (logic)|relational signature]] ''X'', FO[PFP](''X'') is the set of formulas formed from ''X'' using [[First-order logic|first-order connectives and predicates]], [[Second-order logic|second-order variables]] as well as a partial fixed point operator <math>\operatorname{PFP}</math> used to form formulas of the form <math>[\operatorname{PFP}_{\vec{x},P} \varphi]\vec{t}</math>, where <math>P</math> is a second-order variable, <math>\vec{x}</math> a tuple of first-order variables, <math>\vec{t}</math> a tuple of terms and the lengths of <math>\vec{x}</math> and <math>\vec{t}</math> coincide with the arity of <math>P</math>. 

Let {{mvar|k}} be an integer, <math>x, y</math> be vectors of {{mvar|k}} variables, {{mvar|P}} be a second-order variable of arity {{mvar|k}}, and let {{mvar|&phi;}} be an FO(PFP,X) function using {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|P}} as variables. We can iteratively define <math>(P_i)_{i\in N}</math> such that <math>P_0(x)=false</math> and <math>P_i(x)=\varphi(P_{i-1},x)</math> (meaning {{mvar|&phi;}} with <math>P_{i-1}</math> substituted for the second-order variable {{mvar|P}}). Then, either there is a fixed point, or the list of <math>(P_i)</math>s is cyclic.<ref>Ebbinghaus and Flum, p. 121</ref>

<math>[\operatorname{PFP}_{\vec{x},P} \varphi]\vec{t}</math> is defined as the value of the fixed point of <math>(P_i)</math> on <math>\vec{t}</math> if there is a fixed point, else as false.<ref>Ebbinghaus and Flum, p. 121</ref> Since {{mvar|P}}s are properties of arity {{mvar|k}}, there are at most <math>2^{n^k}</math> values for the <math>P_i</math>s, so with a polynomial-space counter we can check if there is a loop or not.<ref>Immerman 1999, p. 161</ref>

It has been proven that on ordered finite structures, a property is expressible in FO(PFP,''X'') if and only if it lies in [[PSPACE]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Abiteboul|first1=S.|last2=Vianu|first2=V.|title=&#91;1989&#93; Proceedings. Fourth Annual Symposium on Logic in Computer Science |chapter=Fixpoint extensions of first-order logic and datalog-like languages |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/lics.1989.39160|year=1989|pages=71–79|publisher=IEEE Comput. Soc. Press|doi=10.1109/lics.1989.39160|isbn=0-8186-1954-6|s2cid=206437693}}</ref>

== Least fixed-point logic ==
Since the iterated predicates involved in calculating the partial fixed point are not in general monotone, the fixed-point may not always exist. 
FO(LFP,X), ''least fixed-point logic'', is the set of formulas in FO(PFP,X) where the partial fixed point is taken only over such formulas {{mvar|&phi;}} that only contain positive occurrences of {{mvar|P}} (that is, occurrences preceded by an even number of negations). This guarantees monotonicity of the fixed-point construction (That is, if the second order variable is {{mvar|P}}, then <math>P_i(x)</math> always implies <math>P_{i+1}(x)</math>).

Due to monotonicity, we only add vectors to the truth table of {{mvar|P}}, and since there are only <math>n^k</math> possible vectors we will always find a fixed point before <math>n^k</math> iterations. The Immerman-Vardi theorem, shown independently by [[Neil Immerman|Immerman]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Immerman|first=Neil|year=1986|title=Relational queries computable in polynomial time|journal=Information and Control|language=en|volume=68|issue=1–3|pages=86–104|doi=10.1016/s0019-9958(86)80029-8|doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[Moshe Vardi|Vardi]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Vardi|first=Moshe Y.|chapter=The complexity of relational query languages (Extended Abstract) |title=Proceedings of the fourteenth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing - STOC '82|date=1982|publisher=ACM|isbn=978-0897910705|location=New York, NY, USA|pages=137–146|citeseerx=10.1.1.331.6045|doi=10.1145/800070.802186|s2cid=7869248}}</ref> shows that FO(LFP,''X'') characterises [[P (complexity)|P]] on all ordered structures.

The expressivity of least-fixed point logic coincides exactly with the expressivity of the database querying language [[Datalog]], showing that, on ordered structures, Datalog can express exactly those queries executable in polynomial time.<ref>Ebbinghaus and Flum, p. 242</ref>

==Inflationary fixed-point logic==
Another way to ensure the monotonicity of the fixed-point construction is by only adding new tuples to <math>P</math> at every stage of iteration, without removing tuples for which <math>P</math> no longer holds. Formally, we define <math>\operatorname{IFP}(\phi_{P,x})</math> as <math>\operatorname{PFP}(\psi_{P,x})</math> where <math>\psi(P,x)=\phi(P,x)\vee P(x)</math>.  

This inflationary fixed-point agrees with the least-fixed point where the latter is defined. Although at first glance it seems as if inflationary fixed-point logic should be more expressive than least fixed-point logic since it supports a wider range of fixed-point arguments, in fact, every FO[IFP](''X'')-formula is equivalent to an FO[LFP](''X'')-formula.<ref> Yuri Gurevich and Saharon Shelah, Fixed-pointed extension of first order logic, Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 32 (1986) 265--280.</ref>

==Simultaneous induction==
While all the fixed-point operators introduced so far iterated only on the definition of a single predicate, many computer programs are more naturally thought of as iterating over several predicates simultaneously. By either increasing the [[arity]] of the fixed-point operators or by nesting them, every simultaneous least, inflationary or partial fixed-point can in fact be expressed using the corresponding single-iteration constructions discussed above.<ref>Ebbinghaus and Flum, pp. 179, 193</ref>

==Transitive closure logic ==
Rather than allow induction over arbitrary predicates, transitive closure logic allows only [[Transitive closure|transitive closures]] to be expressed directly.

FO[TC](''X'') is the set of formulas formed from ''X'' using first-order connectives and predicates, second-order variables as well as a transitive closure operator <math>\operatorname{TC}</math> used to form formulas of the form <math>[\operatorname{TC}_{\vec{x},\vec{y}} \varphi]\vec{s}\vec{t}</math>, where <math>\vec{x}</math> and <math>\vec{y}</math> are tuples of pairwise distinct first-order variables, <math>\vec{t}</math> and <math>\vec{s}</math> tuples of terms and the lengths of <math>\vec{x}</math>, <math>\vec{y}</math>, <math>\vec{s}</math> and <math>\vec{t}</math> coincide.

TC is defined as follows: Let {{mvar|k}} be a positive integer and <math>u,v,x,y</math> be vectors of {{mvar|k}} variables. Then <math>\mathsf{TC}(\varphi_{u,v})(x,y)</math> is true if there exist {{mvar|n}} vectors of variables <math>(z_i)</math> such that <math>z_1=x, z_n=y</math>, and for all <math>i<n</math>, <math>\varphi(z_i,z_{i+1})</math> is true. Here, {{mvar|&phi;}} is a formula written in FO(TC) and <math>\varphi(x,y)</math> means that the variables {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} are replaced by {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}.

Over ordered structures, FO[TC] characterises the complexity class [[NL (complexity)|NL]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Immerman|first=Neil|title=Proceedings of the fifteenth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing - STOC '83 |chapter=Languages which capture complexity classes |date=1983|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1145/800061.808765|pages=347–354|location=New York, New York, USA|publisher=ACM Press|doi=10.1145/800061.808765|isbn=0897910990|s2cid=7503265}}</ref> This characterisation is a crucial part of Immerman's proof that NL is closed under complement (NL = co-NL).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Immerman|first=Neil|date=1988|title=Nondeterministic Space is Closed under Complementation|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1137/0217058|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|volume=17|issue=5|pages=935–938|doi=10.1137/0217058|issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Deterministic transitive closure logic ==
FO[DTC](''X'') is defined as FO(TC,X) where the transitive closure operator is deterministic. This means that when we apply <math>\operatorname{DTC}(\phi_{u,v})</math>, we know that for all {{mvar|u}}, there exists at most one {{mvar|v}} such that <math>\phi(u,v)</math>.

We can suppose that <math>\operatorname{DTC}(\phi_{u,v})</math> is [[syntactic sugar]] for <math>\operatorname{TC}(\psi_{u,v})</math> where <math>\psi(u,v)=\phi(u,v)\wedge \forall x (x=v \vee \neg \phi(u,x))</math>.

Over ordered structures, FO[DTC] characterises the complexity class [[L (complexity)|L]].<ref name=":0" /> 

== Examples ==
[[File:Graph 2-core.svg|thumb|upright=1.35| Red vertices are weak vertices. The remaining vertices form the 2-core of the graph.]]

Define a vertex <math>x</math> to be weak if, with at most one exception <math>y</math>, each of its neighbors <math>z</math> is weak, according to the fixed-point formula <math>W(x)\leftarrow\exists y\forall z\bigl(x\sim z\Rightarrow(y=z\vee W(z))\bigr)</math>. The remaining vertices form the [[Degeneracy (graph theory)|2-core]] of the graph.

The following formula written in Least Fixed-point logic states that the 2-core of a graph is not empty:
<math display=block>\exists t [\operatorname{LFP}_{x,P} \exists y\forall z\bigl(x\sim z\Rightarrow(y=z\vee P(z))\bigr)]t</math>

A graph is connected if there exists a path between every pair of vertices.
The fact that there exists a path between two vertices is the transitive closure of the adjacency relation.
Hence the following formula written in Transitive closure logic states that a graph is connected:
<math display=block>\forall s\forall t [\operatorname{TC}_{x,y} x\sim y]s t</math>

== Iterations ==
The fixed-point operations that we defined so far iterate the inductive definitions of the predicates mentioned in the formula indefinitely, until a fixed point is reached. In implementations, it may be necessary to bound the number of iterations to limit the computation time. The resulting operators are also of interest from a theoretical point of view since they can also be used to characterise complexity classes.

We will define first-order with iteration, <math>\mathsf{FO}[t(n)]</math>; here <math>t(n)</math> is a (class of) functions from integers to integers, and for different classes of functions <math>t(n)</math> we will obtain different complexity classes <math>\mathsf{FO}[t(n)]</math>.

In this section we will write  <math>(\forall x P) Q</math> to mean <math>(\forall x (P\Rightarrow Q))</math> and <math>(\exists x P) Q</math> to mean <math>(\exists x (P \wedge Q))</math>. We first need to define quantifier blocks (QB), a quantifier block is a list <math>(Q_1 x_1, \phi_1)...(Q_k x_k, \phi_k)</math> where the <math>\phi_i</math>s are quantifier-free FO-formulae and <math>Q_i</math>s are either <math>\forall</math> or <math>\exists</math>. If {{mvar|Q}} is a quantifiers block then we will call <math>[Q]^{t(n)}</math> the iteration operator, which is defined as {{mvar|Q}} written <math>t(n)</math> time. One should pay attention that here there are <math>k*t(n)</math> quantifiers in the list, but only {{mvar|k}} variables and each of those variable are used <math>t(n)</math> times.<ref>Immerman 1999, p. 63</ref>

We can now define <math>\mathsf{FO}[t(n)]</math> to be the FO-formulae with an iteration operator whose exponent is in the class <math>t(n)</math>, and we obtain the following equalities:

* <math>\mathsf{FO}[(\log n)^i]</math> is equal to FO-uniform [[AC (complexity)|AC<sup>i</sup>]], and in fact <math>\mathsf{FO}[t(n)]</math> is FO-uniform AC of depth <math>t(n)</math>.<ref>Immerman 1999, p. 82</ref>
* <math>\mathsf{FO}[(\log n)^{O(1)}]</math> is equal to NC.<ref>Immerman 1999, p. 84</ref>
* <math>\mathsf{FO}[n^{O(1)}]</math> is equal to [[P (complexity)|PTIME]]. It is also another way to write FO(IFP).<ref>Immerman 1999, p. 58</ref>
* <math>\mathsf{FO}[2^{n^{O(1)}}]</math> is equal to [[PSPACE]]. It is also another way to write FO(PFP). <ref>Immerman 1999, p. 161</ref>
